Token cost in this setup is driven mainly by: (1) the always-loaded global CLAUDE.md (read into every session's context), (2) memory files loaded each session, (3) large files pulled into context repeatedly, and (4) wasteful in-session churn (loops, re-reads, redundant tool calls). **Directly token-saving (shrink always-loaded context):**

n. **GEN-337** (In Progress, Medium) — "Shrink global CLAUDE.md further — move triggered rules behind hooks." This is the most direct win. The global CLAUDE.md is loaded into *every* session; every rule moved behind an on-demand hook is tokens saved on every turn of every session. It's already in progress.

2\. **GEN-126** (Medium) — "Consolidate overlapping rule clusters in global CLAUDE.md." Same mechanism — less text loaded every session.

3\. **GEN-172 / GEN-173** (Medium) — "Tighten existing rules for conciseness" / "Make conciseness a standard when writing rules." Same file, same always-loaded cost.

4\. **GEN-132** (Medium) — "Purge cross-store duplication between memory store and CLAUDE.md." Both are loaded every session, so duplication is paid twice per session.

5\. **GEN-158 / GEN-291 / GEN-300 / GEN-133** — smaller consolidation/dedup items on the same always-loaded files.

**Indirectly token-saving (reduce in-session waste):**

6\. **GEN-144** (Medium) — "Build in-session loop / edit-churn detector hook." Catches the stuck-loop pattern that burns tokens re-trying. Prevention, not reduction of baseline.

7\. **GEN-138 / GEN-143** — "Transcript-mining token report" + conversation-flow metrics. This is the *measurement* ticket: it tells you where tokens actually go, so you'd stop guessing. Arguably the right *first* step before optimizing.

8\. **GEN-142** (Medium) — "Split the 2,865-line Code.js into modules." Only saves tokens if that file is being read into context often; it's an Invoice-Automation code file, so it helps AI-infra token cost only indirectly.

**The problem is broader than the standalone email.** There are two nags, both firing from day 1:
- **The standalone quiet-day email** (what you got today) — fires once per unset month on the first invoice-free day.

## Root cause

There are actually **two distinct things** going on, and only one is a real problem:

**1. Why the marker still exists (not a bug — expected).** The `.cred-denial-pending-<sid>` marker is created by `permission-denied-log.js` on each classifier denial and deleted by `stop-cred-denial-surface.js` when *that same session's* Stop hook fires. The leftover marker belongs to session `44d9b399` — a **different Claude Code session running concurrently** with this wrap (its transcript was last written at 16:42, so it's still live or only just closed). Its 5 denials fired at 13:36–13:38 (the same classifier-outage storm we've been hitting), and its Stop hook simply **hasn't cleared them yet** because that session hasn't ended a turn cleanly since. So the marker being present is the mechanism working as designed — it's genuinely still pending for the *other* session. It becomes an *orphan* only if `44d9b399` ends abnormally (crash/force-close) without a clean Stop; I can't tell yet whether that will happen.

**2. Why sync warned about it (the actual gap).** `Test-BackupCoverage` in `sync.ps1` walks the `hooks\` folder and warns about any file not in the backup set and not matching an ignore pattern. Its `$IgnoreFiles` list (line 470-473) **already covers the sibling transient markers** — `.loggate-*`, `.config-health-global-marker`, `.settings-health-nudge`, `*.jsonl`, etc. — but **`.cred-denial-pending-*` is missing from that list.** So this per-session transient marker (which by design should never be backed up — it's ephemeral, session-scoped, and self-deleting) trips the coverage warning every time a sync runs while any such marker happens to exist on disk.

So the causal chain is:
- Classifier outage → session `44d9b399` hit 5 denials → `permission-denied-log.js` wrote the marker (correct).
- That session hasn't had a clean Stop since → marker not yet cleared (correct, pending).
- This wrap's sync ran while the marker existed → `Test-BackupCoverage` checked it → `.cred-denial-pending-*` isn't in `$IgnoreFiles` → **warning** (the gap).

**The fix** is a one-line addition: add `.cred-denial-pending-*` to the `$IgnoreFiles` array in `sync.ps1`'s `Test-BackupCoverage`, right alongside `.loggate-*` — declaring it a per-machine transient, same as the other ephemeral markers. That's clearly the right call: this file is inherently session-scoped and self-deleting; it should never be in the backup set, so "ignore" is correct, not "back it up."

One related observation worth noting (not the cause, but adjacent): if a session *does* die abnormally, its marker orphans permanently — nothing sweeps stale `.cred-denial-pending-*` files for dead sessions. The `.loggate-*` markers likely have the same property. That's a minor housekeeping gap, separate from the sync warning.

You asked me to work on **[GEN-329](https://app.notion.com/p/3906e495d07c8145a61eee8450c756d8)** — whether a "due" invoice arriving after the 19th should file in its due month instead of getting bumped to the next month. I dug into the code, ran the reviewer panel on my analysis (converged in 2 rounds), set the ticket to **In Progress**, and here's the plain-language picture.

**The situation:** "To Pay" folders are monthly piles of invoices you still owe. Today the system picks which month's pile a due invoice goes into by the **email arrival date, not the due date printed on the invoice**: if the email lands after the 19th, the invoice drops into **next** month's pile. This is deliberate (it's a stand-in for "when will I actually pay this"), but it ignores the printed due date even when there is one.

- **What triggered the ticket:** Inbal Peer #90022 arrived June 30, printed due date June 30, no service period → landed in **July's** pile purely because 30 is after the 19th.

**Your three choices:**

1\. **Leave it as is** — arrival date decides; after the 19th → next month's pile. #90022 stays in July. Simplest, nothing changes. Downside: an invoice clearly due *this* month but arriving late still lands in next month's pile.

2\. **Narrow fix (my recommendation)** — keep today's rule as the default, but if the invoice's printed due date is in the *same month the email arrived*, don't bump it — keep it in that month's pile.
   - #90022 (arrived June, due June) → **June**. Fixed.
   - Arrived June 28, due July 10 → still July (unchanged).
   - Arrived June 28, due Aug 15 (60-day terms) → still July — **not** flung to August.
   - Smallest change, lowest risk: only touches the exact case you flagged.

3\. **Broad fix** — whenever the invoice prints a due date, use that month regardless of arrival.

Three separate questions — taking them one at a time.

**1. The config-health line — what it means**

The config-health scanner does a mechanical text search for phrases like "the rule above" or "the rule below" — these are considered bad practice in `CLAUDE.md` because if a rule ever gets reordered, "the rule above" silently starts pointing at the wrong thing. So the scanner flags every literal occurrence of that phrase.

It found one at line 123 — but when I looked at what that line actually says, it's *this* rule:

> "...identify the target by a distinctive quoted phrase from it... never by position (**"the rule above/below"**): positional references break silently on reorder..."

That's the rule that *bans* saying "the rule above" — it has to quote the banned phrase in order to explain what not to do, the same way a rule against swearing has to contain the word it's banning. So the scanner's pattern-match is technically correct (the phrase is there) but it's not a real instance of the problem (nothing is actually using it as a broken positional reference). I confirmed that by reading the line myself before reporting it as a false positive, rather than just repeating the scanner's flag.

The second part — `HISTORY.md`, `update-global-rule.ps1`, `update-config.ps1` — is a different check: the scanner also looks for every file/script path mentioned in `CLAUDE.md` and checks if that file exists on disk where it expects. These three don't exist in the folders it checked, so it can't confirm they're there. But it also can't confirm they're *not* there — they're legitimate tools that live on your Google Drive tooling folder, which the scanner doesn't have a fixed path for. So it correctly reports them as "unverified" rather than wrongly declaring them missing. I'm not treating "unverified" as a problem — it's the honest middle state between "confirmed fine" and "confirmed broken," and in this case I recognize all three as real, known tools.

**2. Why the compact-gate block happened**

This project has a safety mechanism: before letting a session compact (summarize and discard detail), a hook checks for a small marker file that says "this session's history has already been written to HISTORY.md." If the marker isn't there, compaction is refused — the point is to make sure nothing gets summarized away before it's durably logged.

Creating that marker is just `touch <path-with-the-session-ID-in-it>`. But Auto Mode has its own separate safety layer — a classifier that inspects *every* command before it runs and blocks anything that looks suspicious, using pattern-matching, not actual understanding of this project's design. It saw a command creating a file with a name like `.loggate-ok-<session-id>` in the Claude config folder and pattern-matched that against "things that disable logging/audit trails" — which is a real and common attack shape (malware creating a file to suppress its own audit log). It has no way to know this is the *opposite* — a file that exists specifically to *prove* logging happened, not to hide it. So it blocked a legitimate, pre-existing, documented step because the filename alone looked suspicious out of context.

## Final converged rule (for global `CLAUDE.md` → Session Learnings)

> In PowerShell, `$LASTEXITCODE` is a session-global automatic variable, so a value a native command (git, npm, curl) sets inside a script invoked with the `&` call operator persists into the caller after the script returns — and PowerShell cmdlets never reset it (only native executables do). If such a script falls off the end or `return`s, the caller reads that native command's exit code as the script's own result — even when the script caught the failure and treated it as non-fatal (e.g. a `git push` downgraded to a warning), producing a false failure. Make every success path yield a deterministic 0: end the script with `exit 0`, or set `$LASTEXITCODE = 0` before returning. Never use `exit` in a script meant to be dot-sourced (`. .\x.ps1`) — there it terminates the caller's entire session; use the `$LASTEXITCODE = 0` form instead. (Distinct from the `$LASTEXITCODE -ne 0` learning above, which is about correctly detecting a native command's failure — not emitting a clean exit code.)

```kusto
          GameID   = tolong(EventData.A_GameID),
          Day      = bin(Timestamp, 1d),
          PlayerAccuracy = todouble(EventData.A_PlayerAccuracy)
| join kind=inner (
    ['events.all']
    | where FullName_Name == "GameStart"
    | project PlayerId = tostring(Entity_Id),
              GameID   = tolong(EventData.A_GameID),
              BoardLayout = tostring(EventData.A_LayoutID)
  ) on PlayerId, GameID
| join kind=inner (
    ['events.all']
    | where FullName_Name == "EnterExperiment" or FullName_Name == "ExperimentVariantChange"
    | where toint(EventData.A_ExperimentId) == 1019
    | where toint(EventData.A_VariantId) == 1
    | distinct PlayerId = tostring(Entity_Id)
  ) on PlayerId
| summarize AvgAccuracy = round(avg(PlayerAccuracy), 4),
            Battles     = count()
        by BoardLayout, Day
| project BoardLayout, Day, AvgAccuracy, Battles
| sort by BoardLayout asc, Day asc
```

**A skill has two parts, and they load at different times:**

1. **Its one-line description** — this is always loaded, sitting in my view every session. It's tiny (cheap). It's basically a label: "notion-howto: Notion technical gotchas."
2. **Its body** — the actual ~10 rules. This is *not* loaded until the skill is **invoked** — meaning either you type `/notion-howto`, or *I* make a deliberate call to open it.

The whole point of moving rules into a skill is to get the body *out* of the always-loaded file (that's the token saving). But that only helps me follow the rules **if the body reliably comes back at the moment I need it.** And that's the weak link.

**Here's the unreliability, concretely.** For the body to be in front of me when I'm doing Notion work, this chain has to fire:

> I'm about to do Notion work → I *recognize* "this is Notion work, there are gotchas I should load" → I *remember* the skill exists → I *choose* to invoke it → *then* the rules load → *then* I apply them.

Every link there depends on **me actively recognizing and deciding** in the moment. Nothing loads on its own. If I don't think to invoke it — because I'm focused on your actual request, not on "should I load a reference file first" — the rules simply aren't there, and I proceed on my default (often wrong) behavior. And here's the nasty part: **when the skill didn't load, there's no gap I can feel.** The rules are just absent; I don't get an error, I don't sense "something's missing." An unloaded skill is invisible. So I'd confidently do the Notion thing the wrong way, exactly as if the rule never existed.

Moving them to a skill trades "present but easy to overlook" for "absent unless I actively fetch them." For always-relevant safety notes, that's often a **worse** bet, not a better one.

**A skill has two parts, and they load at different times:**

1. **Its one-line description** — this is always loaded, sitting in my view every session. It's tiny (cheap). It's basically a label: "notion-howto: Notion technical gotchas."
2. **Its body** — the actual ~10 rules. This is *not* loaded until the skill is **invoked** — meaning either you type `/notion-howto`, or *I* make a deliberate call to open it.

The whole point of moving rules into a skill is to get the body *out* of the always-loaded file (that's the token saving). But that only helps me follow the rules **if the body reliably comes back at the moment I need it.** And that's the weak link.

**Here's the unreliability, concretely.** For the body to be in front of me when I'm doing Notion work, this chain has to fire:

> I'm about to do Notion work → I *recognize* "this is Notion work, there are gotchas I should load" → I *remember* the skill exists → I *choose* to invoke it → *then* the rules load → *then* I apply them.

Every link there depends on **me actively recognizing and deciding** in the moment. Nothing loads on its own. If I don't think to invoke it — because I'm focused on your actual request, not on "should I load a reference file first" — the rules simply aren't there, and I proceed on my default (often wrong) behavior. And here's the nasty part: **when the skill didn't load, there's no gap I can feel.** The rules are just absent; I don't get an error, I don't sense "something's missing." An unloaded skill is invisible. So I'd confidently do the Notion thing the wrong way, exactly as if the rule never existed.

**Contrast that with the file today:** bloated as it is, those rules are *physically in my context every turn.* I might skim past them under load — that's the current problem — but they're *present*, and a careful moment can surface them. Moving them to a skill trades "present but easy to overlook" for "absent unless I actively fetch them." For always-relevant safety notes, that's often a **worse** bet, not a better one.

Picking up where we paused — the next agreed candidate was the **shell reference block** (same hook → prove → delete pattern). Before building, one honest design point that makes shell different from Notion, and it's your call:

**The shell notes fit the prompt-cue hook less well than the Notion ones did.** The Notion hook works because Notion work almost always announces itself in your message ("GEN-123", "Notion", a ticket URL). Shell work usually doesn't — you say "push this" or "fix the script", and I decide mid-turn to run PowerShell. A hook that reads only your message would often miss the cue, and the notes wouldn't be injected when I need them.

The saving grace: all the *dangerous* shell notes (silent mass-deletion, dropped arguments, etc.) stay permanently in the always-loaded file either way — only the recoverable "how-to" detail would move. So a miss costs at most a fixable one-off error, never silent damage.

Options:

1\. **Do the shell block now anyway** — hook fires on shell-ish words (script, git, push, PowerShell, bash, curl...). These appear in many of your messages, so in practice the notes get injected often; misses are possible but low-cost. Cuts ~15 always-loaded lines.

2\. **Skip shell, move to the bigger lever** — compressing/merging the ~50 always-resident behavioral rules (the largest part of the file, ~80% of the remaining benefit). Leave shell for after GEN-334's mid-turn backstop exists, which is the mechanically correct trigger for shell (it would key off me actually calling the shell tool, not your wording).

My recommendation: **option 2**. Shell's natural trigger is the tool call, not your prompt — doing it now with the wrong trigger gives partial coverage for a small saving, while rule compression is the dominant win and needs no new machinery. But option 1 is fine if you want to finish the extraction pattern while it's fresh.

Max/xhigh would be overkill — this isn't a single deep problem, it's ~50 small careful ones, and the `/check` panel gives independent review at the end regardless. Below high (medium/low) I'd likely produce fluent-looking merges that lose edge-case behavior — the exact "silently changes behavior" risk we flagged when ranking this lever.

Picking up where we paused — the next agreed candidate was the **shell reference block** (same hook → prove → delete pattern). Before building, one honest design point that makes shell different from Notion, and it's your call:

**The shell notes fit the prompt-cue hook less well than the Notion ones did.** The Notion hook works because Notion work almost always announces itself in your message ("GEN-123", "Notion", a ticket URL). Shell work usually doesn't — you say "push this" or "fix the script", and I decide mid-turn to run PowerShell. A hook that reads only your message would often miss the cue, and the notes wouldn't be injected when I need them.

The saving grace: all the *dangerous* shell notes (silent mass-deletion, dropped arguments, etc.) stay permanently in the always-loaded file either way — only the recoverable "how-to" detail would move. So a miss costs at most a fixable one-off error, never silent damage.

Options:

1\. **Do the shell block now anyway** — hook fires on shell-ish words (script, git, push, PowerShell, bash, curl...). These appear in many of your messages, so in practice the notes get injected often; misses are possible but low-cost. Cuts ~15 always-loaded lines.

2\. **Skip shell, move to the bigger lever** — compressing/merging the ~50 always-resident behavioral rules (the largest part of the file, ~80% of the remaining benefit). Leave shell for after GEN-334's mid-turn backstop exists, which is the mechanically correct trigger for shell (it would key off me actually calling the shell tool, not your wording).

My recommendation: **option 2**. Shell's natural trigger is the tool call, not your prompt — doing it now with the wrong trigger gives partial coverage for a small saving, while rule compression is the dominant win and needs no new machinery. But option 1 is fine if you want to finish the extraction pattern while it's fresh.

If one of those files is ever renamed, moved, or accidentally emptied, the hook silently injects nothing — forever — and nothing anywhere would notice, because the content no longer lives in the always-loaded rules file.

**Recommended plan — two layers of detection:**

1\. **Warn at the moment it breaks (edit the two hooks).** Today, when a hook can't find its notes file, it stays silent. Change: it instead injects a one-line warning ("notes file missing or empty — content NOT loaded; flag this to Erez") so the very session that hits the breakage sees it and tells you. It never blocks anything — only silence becomes a warning. The shell hook warns once per session; the Notion hook warns on each Notion prompt while broken (deliberately louder; it self-clears the moment the file is fixed).

2\. **A safety-net check at every `/wrap` (extend the existing config-health script).** A fast automatic check (milliseconds, no extra cost) that: (a) every hook registered in settings actually exists on disk; (b) every notes file a hook's code points at exists and is non-empty — read from the hook's actual code, not a hardcoded list, so future hooks are covered automatically; and (c) the reverse: any notes file that no hook points at gets flagged too, which catches renames and also catches the case where the check itself stops understanding a future hook's code — drift becomes a visible finding instead of a silent pass.

3\. **Testing before calling it done:** exercise the broken paths (missing file, empty file, orphaned file, dead hook) against throwaway copies in the scratchpad — real files untouched — then confirm the healthy path still injects the real content, and that the `/wrap` check reports zero findings on the real config.

**The problem the ticket solves:** the Notion and shell reference notes now live in two small files that hooks inject automatically. If one of those files is ever renamed, moved, or accidentally emptied, the hook silently injects nothing — forever — and nothing anywhere would notice, because the content no longer lives in the always-loaded rules file.

**Recommended plan — two layers of detection:**

1\. **Warn at the moment it breaks (edit the two hooks).** Today, when a hook can't find its notes file, it stays silent. Change: it instead injects a one-line warning ("notes file missing or empty — content NOT loaded; flag this to Erez") so the very session that hits the breakage sees it and tells you. It never blocks anything — only silence becomes a warning. The shell hook warns once per session; the Notion hook warns on each Notion prompt while broken (deliberately louder; it self-clears the moment the file is fixed).

2\. **A safety-net check at every `/wrap` (extend the existing config-health script).** A fast automatic check (milliseconds, no extra cost) that: (a) every hook registered in settings actually exists on disk; (b) every notes file a hook's code points at exists and is non-empty — read from the hook's actual code, not a hardcoded list, so future hooks are covered automatically; and (c) the reverse: any notes file that no hook points at gets flagged too, which catches renames and also catches the case where the check itself stops understanding a future hook's code — drift becomes a visible finding instead of a silent pass.

3\. **Testing before calling it done:** exercise the broken paths (missing file, empty file, orphaned file, dead hook) against throwaway copies in the scratchpad — real files untouched — then confirm the healthy path still injects the real content, and that the `/wrap` check reports zero findings on the real config.

4\. **Follow-on, separate approval:** the ticket carries the note that GEN-334's body contains an outdated claim about hook timing (disproven from official docs earlier today). Once GEN-336 is built, I'd draft a correction to GEN-334's body for your approval.

**Main alternative considered:** the ticket's literal proposal — only the `/wrap`-time check, no hook changes. Simpler (one place to build), but a breakage would go unnoticed until the next `/wrap`, with every session in between silently missing the notes; the two-layer version catches it in the moment. **The shell notes fit the prompt-cue hook less well than the Notion ones did.** The Notion hook works because Notion work almost always announces itself in your message ("GEN-123", "Notion", a ticket URL). Shell work usually doesn't — you say "push this" or "fix the script", and I decide mid-turn to run PowerShell. The saving grace: all the *dangerous* shell notes (silent mass-deletion, dropped arguments, etc.) stay permanently in the always-loaded file either way — only the recoverable "how-to" detail would move. So a miss costs at most a fixable one-off error, never silent damage.

Options:

**The problem the ticket solves:** the Notion and shell reference notes now live in two small files that hooks inject automatically. If one of those files is ever renamed, moved, or accidentally emptied, the hook silently injects nothing — forever — and nothing anywhere would notice, because the content no longer lives in the always-loaded rules file.

**Recommended plan — two layers of detection:**

1\. **Warn at the moment it breaks (edit the two hooks).** Today, when a hook can't find its notes file, it stays silent. Change: it instead injects a one-line warning ("notes file missing or empty — content NOT loaded; flag this to Erez") so the very session that hits the breakage sees it and tells you. It never blocks anything — only silence becomes a warning. The shell hook warns once per session; the Notion hook warns on each Notion prompt while broken (deliberately louder; it self-clears the moment the file is fixed).

2\. **A safety-net check at every `/wrap` (extend the existing config-health script).** A fast automatic check (milliseconds, no extra cost) that: (a) every hook registered in settings actually exists on disk; (b) every notes file a hook's code points at exists and is non-empty — read from the hook's actual code, not a hardcoded list, so future hooks are covered automatically; and (c) the reverse: any notes file that no hook points at gets flagged too, which catches renames and also catches the case where the check itself stops understanding a future hook's code — drift becomes a visible finding instead of a silent pass.

3\. **Testing before calling it done:** exercise the broken paths (missing file, empty file, orphaned file, dead hook) against throwaway copies in the scratchpad — real files untouched — then confirm the healthy path still injects the real content, and that the `/wrap` check reports zero findings on the real config.

4\. **Follow-on, separate approval:** the ticket carries the note that GEN-334's body contains an outdated claim about hook timing (disproven from official docs earlier today). Once GEN-336 is built, I'd draft a correction to GEN-334's body for your approval.

**Main alternative considered:** the ticket's literal proposal — only the `/wrap`-time check, no hook changes. Simpler (one place to build), but a breakage would go unnoticed until the next `/wrap`, with every session in between silently missing the notes; the two-layer version catches it in the moment. A full "simulate the hook end-to-end at every `/wrap`" version was also considered and rejected as heavier machinery with its own drift risk — noted as a possible later upgrade.

**Review outcome:** the plan went through the independent review panel and converged in 2 rounds. Round 1 caught two real flaws in my draft — the code-scanning pattern I proposed would have matched the hooks' comments rather than their actual code (it would have "worked" today by coincidence and rotted silently), and I hadn't justified running the check at every `/wrap` when the closest existing precedent runs weekly. Both fixed and verified in round 2. Non-blocking advisories: the repeated Notion-hook warning is a noise trade-off you may want to soften; and the check only guards notes files under the current folder convention — fine for the ticket's scope.

**The problem the ticket solves:** the Notion and shell reference notes now live in two small files that hooks inject automatically. If one of those files is ever renamed, moved, or accidentally emptied, the hook silently injects nothing — forever — and nothing anywhere would notice, because the content no longer lives in the always-loaded rules file.

**Recommended plan — two layers of detection:**

1\. **Warn at the moment it breaks (edit the two hooks).** Today, when a hook can't find its notes file, it stays silent. Change: it instead injects a one-line warning ("notes file missing or empty — content NOT loaded; flag this to Erez") so the very session that hits the breakage sees it and tells you. It never blocks anything — only silence becomes a warning. The shell hook warns once per session; the Notion hook warns on each Notion prompt while broken (deliberately louder; it self-clears the moment the file is fixed).

2\. **A safety-net check at every `/wrap` (extend the existing config-health script).** A fast automatic check (milliseconds, no extra cost) that: (a) every hook registered in settings actually exists on disk; (b) every notes file a hook's code points at exists and is non-empty — read from the hook's actual code, not a hardcoded list, so future hooks are covered automatically; and (c) the reverse: any notes file that no hook points at gets flagged too, which catches renames and also catches the case where the check itself stops understanding a future hook's code — drift becomes a visible finding instead of a silent pass.

3\. **Testing before calling it done:** exercise the broken paths (missing file, empty file, orphaned file, dead hook) against throwaway copies in the scratchpad — real files untouched — then confirm the healthy path still injects the real content, and that the `/wrap` check reports zero findings on the real config.

4\. **Follow-on, separate approval:** the ticket carries the note that GEN-334's body contains an outdated claim about hook timing (disproven from official docs earlier today). Once GEN-336 is built, I'd draft a correction to GEN-334's body for your approval.

**Main alternative considered:** the ticket's literal proposal — only the `/wrap`-time check, no hook changes. Simpler (one place to build), but a breakage would go unnoticed until the next `/wrap`, with every session in between silently missing the notes; the two-layer version catches it in the moment. A full "simulate the hook end-to-end at every `/wrap`" version was also considered and rejected as heavier machinery with its own drift risk — noted as a possible later upgrade.

This is a design/architecture question with a genuine range of options — so before recommending, let me lay out the real alternatives with trade-offs, then converge.

The core problem in one line: **a specific substring of the hook's refusal message became load-bearing, and nothing detects if a future edit removes it.** The question is what "deterministically" should mean here — most of the plausible fixes below are what actually enforce it.

Let me think through the option space breadth-first, since "guard the refusal message" has several genuinely different mechanisms:

**Option A — A test/check that asserts the refusal message still contains the override tokens.**
A tiny check (its own script, or folded into the existing `refs-health` check that already runs at every `/wrap`) greps `auto-approve.js` for the literal strings `CLAUDE_CONFIG_UNLOCK` and the sentinel constant, and fails loudly if either is missing.
- *Strength:* Directly targets the exact failure mode. Deterministic. Cheap. Reuses the already-existing `/wrap` health-check slot, so it fires every session-end automatically.
- *Weakness:* Only fires at `/wrap`, not at edit time — so a bad edit could ship and sit until the next wrap. And a `/wrap` health check is a *detector*, not a *preventer*.

**Option B — A PreToolUse guard that blocks edits to `auto-approve.js` which would remove the override tokens.**
Since `auto-approve.js` is itself a protected/locked file (edited only via `update-config.ps1`), the guard would live in `update-config.ps1`: after writing, re-read and refuse the write if the override tokens vanished.
- *Strength:* Fires at edit time — true prevention, catches it the instant it happens, for the human or agent doing the edit.
- *Weakness:* More invasive (touches the locked update tool), and couples that tool to knowledge of one specific message's content. Slightly brittle if the tokens are ever intentionally renamed.

**Option C — Restore a minimal resident copy of the override in `CLAUDE.md` (undo the single-home-ness).**
Put the actual `CLAUDE_CONFIG_UNLOCK=1` / sentinel string back into the resident rule, so the refusal message is no longer the *only* home.
- *Strength:* Simplest; removes the load-bearing-ness entirely. No new mechanism to maintain.
- *Weakness:* Directly reverses last session's (d) shrink — the whole point was to get that detail *out* of the resident file. And it re-creates a two-copy sync problem (resident + hook could drift). Net-negative against the mission's goal.

**Option D — Do nothing / accept the risk, just annotate the hook with a comment.**
A code comment above the refusal message saying "these tokens are load-bearing — CLAUDE.md points here; don't remove."
- *Strength:* Zero mechanism.
- *Weakness:* Per the standing rule, a comment is documentation, not enforcement — it's only seen when someone opens that spot in the file. Doesn't clear the "deterministically" bar you asked for.

**My lean, and the strongest case for each other option first (per my own check-the-alternatives discipline):**

- *Strongest case for B (edit-time prevention):* it's the only one that stops the loss rather than reporting it after the fact.
- *Strongest case for C (resident copy):* it's the only one that eliminates the fragility instead of guarding it.
- *Strongest case for D:* the risk is genuinely low-frequency (how often does anyone edit that refusal message?).

Weighing those: **C** loses because it fights the mission. **D** loses because it isn't deterministic. Between **A** and **B**, the real question is *detect-at-wrap* vs *prevent-at-edit*. B is stronger in principle, but it means teaching the locked `update-config.ps1` about one hook's message internals — coupling that will itself rot. **A folded into the existing `refs-health` `/wrap` check** is my lean: it's deterministic, it reuses infrastructure that already runs unconditionally every session-end, and the detection window (one session) is acceptable because the resident pointer still works even if the message text drifts — what's at risk is only the *exact tokens*, and a one-session lag to catch that is fine.

There's also a **hybrid A+B worth considering**: the cheap `refs-health` assertion now (A), and file B as a follow-up only if edits to that message ever actually happen. That avoids over-engineering a guard for a rare event while still being deterministic today.

You asked me to **suggest how to deterministically tackle the risk that a future edit strips the break-glass override info out of the lock hook's refusal message** — which last session's `CLAUDE.md` shrink made the *sole* durable home for that info.

**The answer (converged after a 4-round independent review panel on Opus):** a two-layer fix inside [`auto-approve.js`](.claude/hooks/auto-approve.js), each layer guarding a different failure mode.

**Layer 1 — make drift impossible by construction.**
Right now the env-var name `CLAUDE_CONFIG_UNLOCK` is written out *twice* independently — once in the code that actually checks it, once as plain text in the refusal message. Those two copies can silently disagree if someone later renames one. Fix: define the name once as a single named value and have both the check and the message read from that one source. Then the message can never describe an override that doesn't actually work. (The sentinel-file path already works this way — this just applies the same pattern to the env-var name.)

**Layer 2 — a self-test that catches outright deletion.**
Layer 1 stops the message from going *wrong*, but not from being *deleted* entirely. So the hook gets a small self-check that runs every time it fires: it rebuilds its own refusal message and confirms both pieces of override info are actually in it. If either is missing, it **blocks and complains loudly** rather than staying silent — meaning a broken message gets caught on the very next action, not days later. Critically, it's wired to fail in the *safe* direction: a tripped check locks things down (recoverable out-of-band via the emergency override), never quietly waves edits through.

**What it deliberately does *not* cover (stated honestly, not hidden):** if someone keeps the raw values but deletes the surrounding human-readable "here's how to use it" explanation, no automated check can catch that — judging whether prose is still meaningful is beyond deterministic tooling. That residual is accepted.

**Why not the obvious alternative** — just putting the override text back into `CLAUDE.md`: that reverses last session's shrink, re-creates the two-copies-can-drift problem, and works against the whole keep-`CLAUDE.md`-small goal. Rejected.

**Summary:** the key claim that paused GEN-450 turned out to be wrong — there *is* a way to catch a bad claim before you read it — and the suggested design uses it, layered on top of the already-built piece.

## What was done and learned so far on GEN-450

1. **The approved design (2026-07-15).** A "claim-linter": a small guard that runs automatically at the end of each of my turns, scans what I just wrote for confident factual claims that carry no evidence next to them (things like "X isn't available", "it ran cleanly", "GEN-NNN is open"), and if it finds one, tells me to verify it or restate it as unverified. [GEN-451](https://app.notion.com/p/39e6e495d07c81158f8ccc266db5404a) later widened it to also cover stale status claims (Class B), with a 3-week measurement period against known baselines (~4 Class-A + ~2 Class-B slips per week).
2\. **The build (2026-07-16, a prior session).** Two ground-truth probes confirmed the mechanics work, with one important catch: the guard's correction reaches me only at the **start of my next turn** — by then the wrong claim has already reached you. The guard itself was fully built, reviewed twice by independent reviewers plus twice by code review, and passed all 12 live tests — but was **never installed**.
3\. **Why it paused.** You said: "We need to stop wrongful claims BEFORE they are made, not after." The built guard is correct-after, not stop-before. That session concluded no mechanism can intervene before you see my text, and flagged that very conclusion as needing independent verification — which was this session's first job.
4\. **New finding (verified directly against the official documentation this session): that conclusion is half wrong.** True: nothing can stop me *writing* a wrong claim — no mechanism reaches inside the writing itself. False: "nothing sits between writing and your reading." There is a display-time mechanism (`MessageDisplay`) that can change what appears on your screen — so a suspect claim can be **marked with a warning before you ever read it**. The prior session missed it.
5\. **Also verified:** the built guard survived intact (its fingerprint exactly matches its review record — I recomputed both this session), and the vetting process explicitly allows installing an unchanged, already-reviewed file without redoing the review (you still get the approval prompt).

## Suggested design (reviewed to convergence, 2 rounds)

1. **Decision first (yours, below):** does "you never see an unverified claim without a warning mark on it" satisfy what you meant by "before"? The claim still gets written — what changes is that it can't reach you looking trustworthy.
2\. **Install the already-built guard now** (the correct-after piece): near-zero effort, makes me fix flagged claims on the next turn, and produces the measurement data. Worth having under either answer.
3\. **Offer alongside it: a "before-writing" reminder** — a one-line instruction machine-injected at the start of every turn ("verify or mark unverified before asserting"). This is the only lever that acts *before* I write, and it's fundamentally stronger than the existing always-loaded rule that failed, because it's delivered fresh every turn instead of sitting in a long rules file. Small build, light review. Trade-off if installed together with item 2: the 3-week measurement shows their combined effect rather than each piece's own — which only matters if we later want to remove one. My recommendation: install both.
4\. **If you answer yes to the decision: probe the display mechanism first** (one short throwaway test, like the two earlier probes), with pass/fail conditions committed in advance — e.g. if the original text visibly flashes on screen before the marked version replaces it, the idea fails your goal and comes back to you rather than proceeding quietly.
5\. **Only if the probe passes: build the display-time guard** — suspect claims get a visible "⚠ unverified" mark before you read them. This is a full build-and-review effort comparable to the original guard (a full session), and it reuses the same pattern list so the two guards can't drift apart.

## Why the guard can't vet most claims itself — and what it *can* do

1. **For a narrow slice of claims, you're right — it can vet them, and we should add that.** A claim like "GEN-441 is still open" is machine-checkable: a script can pull the ticket number out of the sentence, ask the tracker for the real status (the project already has a working scripted lookup for exactly this), and compare. If they don't match, the mark isn't just "unverified" — it's "**wrong, the ticket actually says X**." That covers the single most common stale-state slip (7 of the 14 logged Class-B cases are exactly this shape). I'd fold it into the guard when the Class-B patterns get built — it's already planned scope, not a new project.
2\. **For everything else, no — because vetting isn't pattern-matching.** The guard is a dumb, instant checklist: "does this sentence look like a factual claim, with no evidence next to it?" But checking whether "this approach can't work" or "the file was deleted" is *true* means opening the right sources, understanding what the claim refers to in this conversation, and judging — that takes an intelligence, not a script.
3\. **Could the guard summon another AI to do that checking at display time? Technically yes, practically no.** A real verification takes tens of seconds to minutes per message; the display guard can't hold the message back meanwhile, so the verdict would land long after you'd read the text. It would also cost a full AI run on every message, the checker would know nothing about our conversation (so it would misjudge what claims even mean), and it can only alter your *screen* — the conversation record would keep the wrong text, creating a confusing split between what you read and what I think I said.
4\. **The design already sends flagged claims to the one agent that** ***can*** **vet them — me, in-session.** The guard's nudge quotes the claim and orders: verify it against the source now, or restate it as unverified. In the soft version I proposed, that lands at the start of my next turn — meaning the vetting waits for your next message.
5\. **The upgrade that matches your question almost exactly is "block mode"** (it was Phase 2 of the original GEN-450 design, deferred): the guard refuses to let me finish my turn while flagged claims stand, so I'm forced to go verify them **immediately and automatically, seconds after the message appears** — no action from you. Four honest caveats, all added to the existing probe step:
6\. It forces another *attempt*, not guaranteed honesty — in principle I could reword the claim to dodge the pattern instead of really checking. The already-planned manual spot-checks watch for exactly that, and the tracker-lookup tier in item 1 is immune to it.
7\. There's a built-in ceiling (after 8 consecutive refusals the system force-ends the turn with a warning) — so the worst case is a claim left standing *with a visible warning*, never an endless loop. I'd have the guard give up after 1–2 attempts anyway; one forced revisit captures most of the value.
8\. Each forced revisit costs an extra model turn on every offending message.
9\. Block mode's exact behavior in this environment is unverified — it goes on the same probe list as the display mechanics (including one specific thing to tune: a session wrap-up summary must not get stuck being blocked).

**Q10 — Cost delivery (server config vs code): ANSWERED.** Game cost is `GameplayBasePrice × StakesMultiplier` and min cost is `GameplayBasePrice × ModeInfo.MinMultiplier`, where `GameplayBasePrice` is populated from `GameplayConfig.Price` delivered via PlayFab config (`GameModeConfigDataProvider.Populate`, `GameData.GetCurrentGameCost()`). So Vs Bonny's "different set of costs" flows through the same config path — dev won't ask *how* costs are delivered. **But** they still need the actual values and confirmation of whether a new mode dimension is added to the config — so this shrinks Q10 to "provide the numbers," which is really Q11.

**Q9 — Skill level / RTP structure: MOSTLY ANSWERED.** `SkillLevelInfo` is keyed per combo = `GameType × GameMode × GameHelper`, and `GetRTP()` = CoinsGained / CoinsSpent lives on that same record. So "Vs Bonny gets its own skill/RTP" just means adding a mode dimension to the combo key, and RTP follows automatically — the same pattern Erez already explained for helpers in the Wheels thread ([MD-3616](https://muuula.atlassian.net/browse/MD-3616)). Dev won't ask "how does skill/RTP work"; they *may* still ask for the difficulty/normalization values (the `[Bonny 0.8 | Online 1]` calibration).

**Q3 — FTUE-seen flag storage: ANSWERED.** FTUE completion is tracked in `FTUEKeys.FTUEStepKey` (enum) with state persisted in `CachedFTUEData` (local `PersistentData`, `PersonalData=true`), plus a server path (`MarkFTUEDoneOperation` / `FTUEDoneRedisFieldWrapper`) for server-tracked ones. New Vs Bonny FTUEs would be new enum entries in the existing system. Dev won't ask "where do FTUE flags live" — the mechanism is established and local-cache-based, consistent with the [MD-3620](https://muuula.atlassian.net/browse/MD-3620) answer.

Now I have everything verified. Here's the grounded answer.

## First — does moving it actually save tokens?

**Yes.** The project `CLAUDE.md` is loaded in full at the start of every Documentation-project session (you can see it injected in my context this very session). Every line in its FORMATTING section is paid for on every turn of every session, whether or not I'm writing a ticket. So a formatting section that's only relevant *when authoring a ticket* is being paid for constantly but used rarely — that's exactly the "always-loaded cost for a sometimes-need" pattern that's worth moving.

## Is there a better home? Yes — and the project already uses it

There's a proven pattern sitting right here: **`hooks/refs/*.md` + an injection hook.** I verified how it works — `inject-jira-refs.js` watches your prompt, and *only when the turn looks like Jira work* (a ticket key like `MD-1234`, the word "jira", or an `atlassian.net` URL) it injects `refs/jira.md` for that one turn. There are already four such ref files (jira, notion, shell, editing), each moved *out* of the always-loaded global `CLAUDE.md` precisely to cut per-session cost. This is the established, working mechanism for "load it only when relevant."

So the better home is: **a `refs/ticket-formatting.md` file, injected by a hook that fires on ticket-authoring cues** — the same cues the Jira hook already uses (MD-key, atlassian.net, "confluence"). When you're writing a ticket, the rules load; when you're not, they cost nothing.

## But — one honest caveat that matters

The ref-injection mechanism has a **known blind spot**, documented in the Jira hook itself (lines 6–8): it fires on `UserPromptSubmit`, so it only sees your *prompt*. **Ticket formatting work that arises mid-turn — without a prompt cue — isn't covered.** And ticket-authoring very often arises mid-turn: I read code, then draft a ticket, all in one turn where your prompt was just "document feature X." In those turns the prompt may carry no `MD-` key or "jira" token, so the hook wouldn't fire, and I'd draft the ticket *without* the formatting rules loaded.

That's the real tradeoff, and it's the same reasoning the review panel and the load-tier rule apply: **a pointer/hook can't guard a "forgot-to-check" failure.** Formatting rules that must shape a draft I produce *while* drafting are most reliably present if they're always-loaded. The refs that were moved out (Jira/Notion/shell gotchas) are different in kind — they're *reactive* (you hit a gotcha when using that tool, and the tool use itself is the reliable cue). Ticket formatting is *generative* — it has to be in mind before I write, with no reliable tool-cue.

## My recommendation

Given your token concern is real but the reliability risk is also real, the proportionate answer is a **split by trigger-reliability, not a wholesale move:**

- **Keep always-loaded (in project `CLAUDE.md`):** nothing extra — actually, the strongest case is to keep the whole FORMATTING section where it is, because every rule in it is generative-at-draft-time.
- **The lower-cost alternative, if you want the savings:** move the FORMATTING section to `refs/ticket-formatting.md`, injected on ticket cues, **and** add the `document-feature` skill (your main ticket-drafting workflow, which *is* a reliable cue) to read it as an explicit step. That closes most of the mid-turn gap — because when you invoke `/document-feature`, the skill itself pulls the rules in, cue or no cue. The residual gap is ad-hoc ticket edits outside that skill.

**Honest bottom line:** the savings are modest (the FORMATTING section is ~8 lines) and the reliability cost is non-trivial (formatting rules that silently don't load when drafting mid-turn produce badly-formatted tickets you'd have to catch manually). I'd **keep it always-loaded** unless the section grows a lot larger — at which point the refs-file + `document-feature`-step approach becomes worth the residual risk. This is a genuine judgment call on your risk tolerance, so I'm not deciding it for you.

It silently **no-ops** — reports success, changes nothing — when the target text spans more than one "rich-text segment." # /suggest — form the smallest proposal that meets every goal

```markdown
A single checklist for **forming** a non-routine recommendation before it reaches Erez.
Its whole point is to catch over-engineering and missing alternatives **at formation
time** — before a proposal exists in a shape you have already anchored on, and before a
`/check` review round is spent. `/suggest` **forms**; `/check` **reviews** the formed
proposal independently. They are two stages, not duplicates.

Apply this to the proposal as a whole (not just the part you thought of first), then hand
off to `/check` per the existing global-CLAUDE.md "run /check before presenting" bridge.

## When this applies

- A non-routine recommendation, design, architecture, trade-off, or course-of-action call
  you are about to present — whether Erez asked a question or you are proposing unprompted.
- NOT routine requests, plain factual lookups, or finished mechanical tasks — answer those
  directly (same carve-out as the global rules).

## The checklist

1. **Smallest design first.** Start from the bare list of goals the proposal must meet.
   Build the *minimal* thing that meets every one of them, and add nothing no named goal
   requires. If a part isn't traceable to a stated goal, cut it. (This is the anti-over-
   engineering step — the reason this skill exists.)
2. **At least one real alternative, with trade-offs.** Never present a single answer to a
   design/architectural question as if it were the only option. Give a genuine alternative
   and what each choice costs.
3. **Steelman every option you are *not* recommending.** Before recommending one option
   over others, write down the strongest reason to choose each of the others. If you can't
   find a strong reason for an option, you haven't thought about it hard enough yet — go
   think harder before recommending.
4. **First pass is a draft — rate confidence, re-examine if low.** Treat the first version
   as a draft; rate your confidence internally; if it isn't high, re-examine from scratch
   before presenting. (This discipline is owned by the always-loaded "For any non-routine
   answer … treat the first pass as a draft" rule, which fires on a wider set of answers
   than proposals — this is a pointer to it, not a restatement.)
5. **Verify load-bearing claims before asserting them.** Any capability, number, config
   fact, or claim the proposal rests on must be checked against a live source, not stated
   from memory or a summary. (Owned by the always-loaded "Verify before asserting" rule —
   cited here, not restated, because it fires on far more than proposals.)
6. **Hand off to `/check`.** Once the proposal is formed, run it through `/check` per the
   global rule ("run the /check skill on the proposed answer before presenting it"). The
   self-minimize in step 1 is your first pass; `/check`'s Holistic lens is the independent
   backstop — expect it to re-derive minimality from scratch, and don't treat your own
   step-1 pass as making that redundant.

## What this skill does NOT own

To avoid three drifting homes for the same behavior, this skill **cites** rather than
copies the always-loaded rules whose trigger surface is wider than "forming a proposal":
the draft/confidence rule (step 4), the verify-before-asserting rule (step 5), and the
one-item-at-a-time / plain-terms presentation rule (which governs how *any* item goes to
Erez for approval, not only proposals). Those stay in the global `CLAUDE.md`. This skill
owns only the formation discipline that is specific to building a proposal: steps 1–3.

## Relationship to `/check` (read once)

`/check` already asks, in its Holistic lens, "is each part of the proposal actually needed
(smallest design that still meets every goal)?" That is the same test as step 1 here, run
at a different stage: step 1 is the cheap self-pass at formation; `/check`'s lens is the
independent review. This is deliberate layering (self-check then independent check), not
duplication — but if either wording is ever edited, update both so they keep describing the
same test.
```

- **Why a prompt and not an outright block:** a command-line call hides its details (the actual change can be in a separate file the hook can't open), so the hook can only tell "this is a Notion write," not *which* kind. A prompt is the right level — it guarantees you see and approve any write, without wedging legitimate ones that have no other path.

Both options keep the existing failure queue — a genuinely failed upload still gets logged and surfaced to you next session. Option 2 doesn't lose the "you'll be told if a backup failed" safety net. It only loses the *precision of the retry timing*, not the *awareness*.

1. **Byte-cursor only (template as-is):** shows each pending marker once, then advances past it. ✗ Wrong — this resolves on first sight; it can't represent "still pending, check again next time," which is exactly what a survival check needs.
2. **Reader writes resolution back into the queue** (flip a `surfaced`/`resolved` flag in-place). ✗ Violates the append-only-never-write invariant the template's comments call load-bearing; races the writer.
3. **Separate reader-owned *state* file** (not just a byte cursor): the surfacer reads ALL pending markers each session, and keeps its own JSON state `{markerId → {firstSeen, lastChecked, status}}`. Each session it re-checks artifact existence for every not-yet-resolved marker; clears (marks resolved in its own state) on survival, alerts on kill. The queue stays strictly append-only; all mutation is in the reader's own file. ✓ This is the append-only-safe way to hold richer-than-cursor state, and it's the natural generalization of the cursor idea.
4. **A minimum-dwell before resolving** (e.g. don't clear until the marker is ≥ N hours/1 session-gap old), so "survived" means "survived real elapsed time," not "existed at the very next startup seconds later." ✓ needed — folds into option 3's state.

Let me think through the options for how the surfacer tracks what it has already shown, since this is the foundational primitive:

**Option B — a separate "high-water mark" cursor file.** The surfacer records how far into the queue it has read (e.g. byte offset or a count of lines consumed), stored in its own small file it fully owns. Next session, it reads only lines past the mark. The queue file itself is never touched — stays truly append-only. No race with the sweep writer. This matches the "read+mark" intent without rewriting the shared file. The `surfaced` field in the record becomes effectively vestigial (or a within-file hint), but the cursor is the real mechanism.

**Option C — the surfacer moves consumed lines to an archive file** (read all, show unsurfaced, append them to `backup-sweep-failures.archive.jsonl`, then truncate the live queue). Rejected: truncating the live queue races the concurrent sweep exactly like Option A.

The only thing that costs standing tokens is the *one always-loaded file*. Everything it points to is lazy. So:
- **Flat index:** N learnings = N lines always-loaded.
- **Index-of-indexes:** M topic lines always-loaded; each topic file (lazy) lists its own learnings; each learning body (lazy) is a third level.

So hierarchy trades **standing token cost** for **retrieval reliability** — the deeper you bury a learning, the cheaper it is to hold and the easier it is to never surface. That trade is fine for topic-clustered learnings (a "shell gotcha" reliably fires on shell work) and bad for cross-cutting ones (a general "prefer X over Y" heuristic has no topic to file under — it just sinks).

Sharp question — and the answer depends entirely on *how* A is done. Done naively, **yes, it leaks.** Done correctly, **no.** Let me be precise, because this is exactly the kind of thing worth getting right.

**How it would leak (the naive way):** if I read the sheet cell and print the token to stdout — or set it in one command and inspect it in another — the value lands in a tool *result*, which becomes part of my context and the session transcript. That's a real leak: it'd sit in the transcript, and if this session were ever attached to a feedback report (like the `/feedback` we just discussed), it'd travel. So a naive A is genuinely unsafe.

**How to do A without leaking:** keep the token inside a **single shell invocation**, from read to use, and never emit it. The token flows: secure sheet → a shell variable → the `curl` Authorization header → discarded when the command ends. It's never printed, never returned in a result. The only thing that comes back to my context is curl's *response* (the created comment's URL), not the token. This is exactly how the Notion-token pattern already works — `notion-ticket-lookup.ps1` reads the token from the vault and passes it to curl within one script, and the token never appears in any result. Same discipline.

Concretely, the safeguards:
- Read the sheet and extract the cell, assign to a variable, and reference `$VAR` only inside the `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAR"` — all in **one** Bash call.
- **Never** `echo`/`Write-Output` the variable; never `curl -v` (logs headers); print only curl's JSON response piped through a filter that extracts just the comment URL.
- The command *string itself* gets logged to `deferred-calls.jsonl`, but it contains `$VAR`, not the literal token — and that log is redacted for token-shaped strings anyway.

**But there's a residual risk even done right, and I should name it:** the *command text* I write will be visible in my context and the transcript (that's unavoidable — I author it). As long as it references the variable and never the literal value, the secret itself doesn't appear. The failure mode is if the sheet-read step accidentally surfaces the value (e.g., the extraction prints the whole row). I'd guard that by extracting precisely and routing only the non-secret output back.

There's also a subtlety with *your* secure sheet specifically: it's a `.gsheet` (Google Drive). Reading it might go through the Google Drive MCP tools, whose **results return to my context** — if that tool returns the cell value, the token *is* in a tool result, leaked, regardless of my shell hygiene. That's the part I can't fully guarantee is leak-proof, because I don't control what the Drive tool echoes back. That's a real strike against A.

Given that — my recommendation shifts:

**What GEN-566 changes, in plain terms.** When we build a watchdog (something that inspects what I write, or a command I'm about to run, and decides to allow it, block it, or flag it), our own build checklist currently says: test it by running it for real. It does *not* say the test material has to be real. So the person building it writes test sentences — and unconsciously writes them in wording that avoids the very phrases real work contains. That already bit us twice: a watchdog passed 25 out of 25 hand-written tests and then, in real use, wrongly blocked essentially every message where I reported a ticket, because no hand-written test had used the words real ticket reports actually need.

The fix adds a requirement in two places in the checklist:

1. **Test it on real material.** If the watchdog already has a log of its own past decisions, run all of it. Otherwise take at least 10 real past messages, deliberately including ones that *should* trip it and ones that must *not*. Samples picked because they're easy to pass don't count.
2. **One false alarm on real material means the test fails.** I can't quietly downgrade that to "minor" — I have to show you the count and you decide whether to accept it.
3. **Report it to you when I ask for approval**, with the numbers — not a vague "testing passed."
4. **Blank out anything sensitive** before quoting real material into a record, since real commands can contain passwords or tokens.

**Can a sub-agent solve the anchoring problem? Partly — but there's a hard mechanical wall.**

What a sub-agent *does* give you: genuine cold context. A spawned agent gets **only the prompt you hand it** — it cannot see the first pass's findings, the fixes, or the conversation. That's real, true blindness — exactly the independence the same-session second pass lacks. On that axis, yes, a sub-agent solves it.

And `/code-review` reviews the live working tree via git/shell.

So a sub-agent can be a **cold reviewer**, but it cannot be a cold **`/code-review` run**. It would be reading the diff with Read/Grep/Glob and reasoning — a capable static review, but not the same tool the first pass used, and it can't do the live-probe things (`node --check`, planting a token) that caught the actual GEN-382 fail-opens.

That gives us a clear option space:

**Option 1 — Second pass as a cold sub-agent reviewer (static).** Spawn a fresh agent, hand it only the diff + the adversarial brief, get findings back, you apply fixes in the main session. **Gains:** true context independence — the anchoring weakness is genuinely gone. **Costs:** it's a static diff read, not a `/code-review` invocation and not live-fire; and it's more orchestration wiring in the skill (spawn, collect, merge, apply). Net: trades a *stronger* review mechanism (real `/code-review` + live-verify) for *stronger independence*. Given that Step 4 (live-verify) already exercises the runtime separately, the lost live-probe isn't fully lost — but the second pass is weaker as a *review*.

**Option 2 — The one I'd actually reach for: a fresh, separate session.** The cleanest way to get a genuinely cold second `/code-review` — full tool access, real live working tree, real `node --check`, *and* zero context bleed — is to run it in a **new session** (or after `/clear`), pointed at the same working copy. More friction, and it breaks the "one skill, start to finish" shape.

**Option 3 — Keep same-session + adversarial brief (the converged design).** Weakest independence, but full `/code-review` power, live-fire intact, zero orchestration cost, and empirically it *did* catch the bugs.

The **classifier** here is Claude Code's **auto-mode permission classifier** — a safety check that runs *before* certain tool calls to decide whether they're safe to auto-approve, block, or route to you for a prompt. It's the thing that produced those "temporarily unavailable" / "Stage 2 classifier error" messages.

Here's the fuller picture:

**What it is.** When Claude Code runs in "auto" permission mode, not every tool call I make is waved through automatically. For calls that aren't obviously read-only-and-safe (running a shell command that changes state, writing outside the working directory, etc.), the harness sends the proposed action to a **separate, server-side classifier model** whose only job is to judge: is this safe to allow, should it be blocked, or should the user be asked? It's a distinct model from the one I'm running on (Opus 4.8) — you don't pick it with `/model`; Anthropic configures it on the server.

**Why it exists.** It's a guardrail so that in auto mode, risky actions get gated without you having to approve every single call by hand. It's a different layer from the `auto-approve.js` *hook* (your own local rules, like the chain-guard that blocked `cd && git push`). The hook is your custom policy; the classifier is Anthropic's built-in safety model. A call can be stopped by either.

**What "fails closed" means.** When the classifier model itself is momentarily unreachable or overloaded (which is what "claude-opus-4-8 is temporarily unavailable" / "Stage 2 classifier error" signals), it can't return a safe/unsafe verdict. Rather than guess and risk allowing something dangerous, the system **refuses the call** — it errs on the side of blocking. That's "failing closed": when unsure, deny rather than allow. That's why the block message says "usually transient — retrying often succeeds": once the model is reachable again a moment later, the identical call gets a real verdict and goes through.

**Why this isn't a real denial.** A genuine denial is a *decision* — "this action is unsafe, no." That's deterministic: retry it and it fails again. What happened twice this turn (the git push, the marker write) was the classifier being temporarily *unavailable to decide at all* — proven by the identical retry succeeding within seconds. Availability failure, not judgment. That's the distinction we worked out and recorded on GEN-394, and it's why neither counts as the GEN-316 case (which is specifically the classifier *wrongly deciding* to deny a call it should have allowed).

Short version: it's an Anthropic-run safety model that pre-screens risky tool calls in auto mode; when it's briefly down it blocks-by-default, and a retry a second later normally clears it.

The wrap-up procedure (`/wrap`, Step 4) requires two coordinated writes to a project's `HISTORY.md`: prepend the new dated entry to the body, **and** prepend a matching one-line entry to the `## Table of contents`. Multiple failures surfaced in a single day on `Improve AI Infra/HISTORY.md`:
1. **Missing TOC line (single-session):** a wrap prepended the `(4)` body entry but never added its TOC line.

## Directions to consider (settle during design; run `/check` before building)

That's a worse outcome than the problem we started with. A backup safety net that can strand you is not a good safety net.

So the answer to your question is: **it should not work that way, and I'd argue against building it that way.** Here's the distinction that resolves it —

There are two very different reasons a backup can "fail," and they must be treated oppositely:

1\. **A gap — something isn't *set up* to be backed up.** A new file/folder sits outside the backup set (your `notion-fetch-staleness.js` case), or a new project isn't a git repo yet, or has no remote. This is a *configuration* problem, it's *fixable in seconds*, and leaving it unresolved means silent permanent loss. **This is worth being loud and stubborn about** — surface it unmissably, and don't let it slip by unnoticed.

2\. **A transient operational failure — backup is set up correctly but the *act* of backing up failed right now.** Network down, GitHub 500, credential expired, Drive unmounted. This is *not your fault*, often *not fixable at that moment*, and — critically — **not data loss**: the work is still safe on your local disk, and the very next successful sync/push captures it. The existing config sync already treats git failures this way on purpose (warn, don't block, retry next time — it's designed so being offline doesn't break anything).

Blocking `/wrap` is the right response to **(1)** and the wrong response to **(2)**. Conflating them is how you get stranded.

So the enforcement I'd actually propose, and I think it fully meets "airtight" without the hostage risk:

- **Gaps (case 1): loud + unskippable.** At session end, enumerate everything and check *coverage* — is each file/folder/project *configured* to be backed up? Any gap gets surfaced in the wrap output prominently and **won't clear until it's resolved** (resolved = either added to the backup set / repo, or you explicitly mark it "don't back this up"). This is cheap to fix, so it won't strand you — and it's the exact failure that hit you.
- **Transient failures (case 2): loud, retried, never blocking.** If the *act* of pushing fails, wrap still completes, but it tells you unmissably: "your work is safe locally but did NOT reach GitHub/Drive — retry when you're back online," and the next session's start retries automatically and re-warns if still unpushed. You're never stuck, and you're never in the dark.

The result: you can't *silently* lose data (a gap can't slip past, and a failed push can't pretend it succeeded), but a dead network can never trap you in a session you can't close.

There's one honest judgment call inside case (1): what counts as "resolved" for a gap. If the only way to clear it is *successfully backing it up*, then a gap discovered while you're also offline could still block you. The fix is to let you clear a gap by **either** backing it up **or** explicitly deferring/excluding it — so the gate is on *you having made a decision*, never on the network cooperating. That keeps it airtight (nothing slips unnoticed) while keeping the exit always in your hands.

Does that resolve your concern — block only on unresolved *setup gaps* (fixable in seconds, or dismissible by an explicit choice), never on *transient backup failures* (which warn + retry but always let you wrap)? If yes, that's the core design decision settled, and I'll move to the scope question next.

You asked: if you choose (b), what problems can it cause for multiple sessions working on the same project, and what are its limitations — considering current needs and future ones (multiple PCs, other tools like Cursor)?

This answer went through the independent review panel (3 reviewers, converged in 2 rounds — round 1 surfaced six real gaps, all fixed below).

**Multiple sessions on the same project, same PC (your current reality)** — manageable; the frictions are real but none lose data:

1. Collisions. Git allows one bookkeeping write at a time, so two sessions' backup steps can collide; the loser retries. Worst case: a snapshot is delayed a few minutes — your files are safe on disk the whole time. The design shrinks collisions by creating snapshots without touching the shared working state, and by giving each session its own snapshot record, so sessions don't fight over the same one. Collisions that still happen only delay, never corrupt.

2\. Noisy history. Backup snapshots would clutter your curated project history. The design keeps them in a separate backup record inside the same repo, out of your normal view — main history stays exactly as `/wrap` leaves it. One fact to know: these backup records also don't show on GitHub's website view (they're reachable and restorable by git), so "I don't see it on GitHub.com" won't mean "not backed up."

3\. Safety rules the machinery must obey: it only reads and pushes — never anything that changes working files, so it can never disturb a session mid-work; every snapshot must be pushed to a named record, never left dangling locally (git eventually garbage-collects unattached snapshots); and if a repo is mid-merge-conflict, the backup step flags it loudly instead of silently snapshotting conflict debris.

**Multiple PCs (future)** — git handles this well: each machine (and session) writes snapshots under its own name, so machines never fight over the same record; real work still flows between PCs through normal git push/pull. Worst case is visible divergence you reconcile — git refuses to silently overwrite diverged work (verified). By contrast, a Drive mirror across two PCs resolves concurrent edits by making conflict-copies — duplicate files you clean up by hand. Honest costs: each new PC needs the backup machinery installed (should be a one-script install), and the catch-all repo for brand-new folders needs entries labeled by originating machine so "promote to its own repo?" triage stays clear.

**Cursor / other tools — the biggest limitation of (b) as originally designed.** The Claude hook only fires when *Claude* writes a file. Edits from Cursor, Notepad, Unity etc. are invisible to it — they'd wait for the next Claude session, possibly days. That's the exact silent-narrowing this ticket exists to kill. The fix: add a **scheduled sweep** — Windows runs the same backup pass every ~15–30 minutes, regardless of which tool made the change. Three honest caveats about the sweep, each with a design answer:

4\. Sleep gap. Scheduled tasks don't run while the PC sleeps — "Claude closed + laptop lid shut" could silently disable both layers at once. Answer: configure catch-up-on-wake, plus a dead-man's-switch — if no sweep succeeded within a few expected intervals, you get an unmissable notice. Live-tested at build, not assumed.

5\. Torn files. A timed sweep can catch a file mid-save and snapshot a half-written version that looks like a good backup. Answer: only snapshot files unchanged for a minute or so; and since older snapshots are never overwritten, a torn latest means you restore the one before it. Residual risk stated honestly: the very last moments before a crash may only exist torn.

6\. Whether a scheduled task on this machine can push to GitHub with stored credentials is standard-but-not-guaranteed — live-tested at build.

**A real choice this opens — sweep-only, or hook + sweep:**
- **Sweep-only (simpler):** one mechanism, no session-collision handling to build, less machinery to silently break. Cost: work is exposed up to ~15–30 minutes before it's backed up.
- **Hook + sweep (faster):** Claude's work backed up within seconds; sweep covers everything else. Cost: the extra plumbing (per-session records, collision handling) must be built and kept working.
My lean: start sweep-only — it alone delivers the airtight floor, and simplicity is itself protection. Add the hook later only if the ~20-minute window ever bothers you. Genuinely your call.

**Other inherent limitations of the git path:**

7\. Ignored files aren't backed up — git inherits each repo's ignore list (today: only regenerable node_modules); the design must audit ignore lists and surface anything non-regenerable rather than silently skip.

8\. Suspected secrets sit unprotected until you decide — fail-closed scanning (your decision) means a flagged file is pushed nowhere until you rule; the flag must be loud.

9\. Large files — GitHub rejects files over 100 MB. Irrelevant now; a future heavy-asset project (game builds, video) needs Git LFS or a different destination, detected and surfaced rather than failing silently.

10\. Snapshot buildup — frequent snapshots accumulate; years from mattering for your text projects, but a retention policy from day one compacts old ones (the permanent record stays the curated `/wrap` commits).

11\. Network dependency — covered by your never-block + loud-notice + retry decision; the sweep retries automatically every interval.

12\. One remote basket — everything lands in one GitHub account; account lockout is the residual risk, coverable by the optional Drive second destination (pending its live test).

**Scope note:** this covers your project folders. The `.claude` config universe stays on its separate existing mechanism (`sync.ps1` to Drive + its git history) — its own multi-PC story isn't analyzed here.

**Bottom line:** multi-session on one PC — workable, worst case is delay not loss. Multi-PC — git is the strongest option here (visible reconciliation, no silent overwrites), at the cost of a per-machine install. Other tools — the hook alone would NOT cover them; the scheduled sweep is what makes (b) tool-agnostic. None of this breaks (b) for your stated needs.

**Two decisions now sit with you:** the main one — (a) move to Drive / (b) git-based backup / (c) Drive folder-mirror; and if (b), the sub-choice — sweep-only or hook + sweep (I lean sweep-only to start).

**The risk you're naming is real.** If "airtight" means *the session literally cannot `/wrap` until every file is successfully backed up*, then any backup failure becomes a hostage situation: GitHub is down, your network drops, a git credential expired, a merge conflict on the config-history repo, Google Drive File Stream is unmounted — and now you can't close a session that has nothing wrong with it *except* the backup layer, at possibly midnight, with kids to deal with. There are two very different reasons a backup can "fail," and they must be treated oppositely:

1\. **A gap — something isn't *set up* to be backed up.** A new file/folder sits outside the backup set (your `notion-fetch-staleness.js` case), or a new project isn't a git repo yet, or has no remote. This is a *configuration* problem, it's *fixable in seconds*, and leaving it unresolved means silent permanent loss. **This is worth being loud and stubborn about** — surface it unmissably, and don't let it slip by unnoticed.

2\. **A transient operational failure — backup is set up correctly but the *act* of backing up failed right now.** Network down, GitHub 500, credential expired, Drive unmounted. This is *not your fault*, often *not fixable at that moment*, and — critically — **not data loss**: the work is still safe on your local disk, and the very next successful sync/push captures it. The existing config sync already treats git failures this way on purpose (warn, don't block, retry next time — it's designed so being offline doesn't break anything).

Blocking `/wrap` is the right response to **(1)** and the wrong response to **(2)**. Conflating them is how you get stranded.
